He proposed that only green plant parts could carry out the process of photosynthesis. What about plants having variously coloured leaves? How is it that new leaves which look dark red in colour in several plants turn green? Do plants having reddish or yellowish leaves also carry out photosynthesis? What made plants carry out photosynthesis while even green coloured animals like some birds could not? Such questions remained as challenges until scientists could isolate the green coloured substance from plant parts and study its nature. Establishment of Ingenhousz’s proposition become possible in the year 1817 due to the work of two scientists Pelletier and Caventou. They obtained an extract of the green coloured substance and named it ‘chlorophyll’ meaning green leaf. It was also found that pigments in addition to chlorophyll, carotenoids and phycobilins could also aid in the process of photosynthesis by passing on the energy of sunlight trapped by them to chlorophyll. Scientists have come to know that energy released during oxygen formation is reutilised. This means that plants must be able to absorb energy as they produce oxygen. x Where did this energy come from? A Dutch scientist, Jan Ingenhousz (1730-1799), found the answer. To know about how the plants release oxygen he studied continuously. In 1779, he noticed that plants form oxygen only in the presence of light. In an experiment with the aquatic plant, Hydrilla (submerged, rootless water plant), he observed that in bright sunlight, small bubbles were formed around the green parts while in the dark they did not form. He also found that the gas present in the bubbles was oxygen. It was further confirmed when Engelman in the early 20 th century ingeniously detected the point of maximum rate of photosynthesis. He used a group of algae and exposed it to different colours of light the colours that we see in a rainbow. Then he used oxygen sensitive bacteria and found that they crowd around areas illuminated with bright red and blue rays of light. This led to the studies on effect of light on photosynthesis, the role of different coloured compounds called pigments in plants and the utilization of light energy. parsed_output.answer: To study the presence of starch in leaves, the following process is followed in the laboratory: first, a leaf is boiled in water to kill any existing enzymes and then boiled in methylated spirit to remove chlorophyll. After that, the leaf is spread on a petridish and a few drops of iodine solution are added. If starch is present, the leaf turns bluish-black. This indicates the presence of starch, which is a product of photosynthesis.
